items.quote: durst not openly professe the truth
items.note: The milder Galenists hold back what they think true, for fear of being excommunicated.

items.quote: these with open Arms will most readily imbrace this so long look't for, and desired light
items.note: Croll expects these Galenists to welcome what he offers, which he calls a long-desired light.

items.quote: these things should be made common for publick use
items.note: Croll presents his work as making things common for public use and foresees envy at this.

items.quote: which notwithstanding are secretly reserved for their uses
items.note: Envious men coldly praise these things in public while secretly keeping them for their own use.

items.quote: When envy and hatred give counsell, the Judgement is nothing worth.
items.note: Margin maxim: judgement driven by envy is worthless.

items.quote: virtue can never be found without the marks and wounds of envy
items.note: Croll holds that envy always follows virtue and those who work for the common good.

items.quote: I study not to please all, for neither all men nor all things please me.
items.note: Margin note in the first person: Croll does not aim to please everyone.

items.name: Comaedian
items.quote: according to the Comaedian, there can be nothing more unjust then these leud haters of Chymistry, and despisers of wisdome
items.note: A judgement on the haters of Chymistry is credited to 'the Comaedian'.

items.quote: being plunged into Scholasticall dirt and dust over head and ears
items.note: Croll describes the dull opponents as sunk in school learning.

items.quote: There is a two-fold Alchymy. Naturall, much esteemed by Artist. Sophisticall, as much detested by them.
items.note: The margin sets apart two kinds of Alchymy, a natural one valued by the Artist and a sophistical one rejected.

items.quote: shamelesly to scoff at this Divine Art
items.note: Chymistry is named a Divine Art.

items.quote: who tremble at the very name of Chymistry
items.note: The opponents are called contemners of Natures secrets who fear the very name of Chymistry.

items.quote: trample upon the Truth, and those Pearls cast before them
items.note: The truth offered is called pearls cast before the opponents; interpreted: a figure for something precious given to those who cannot value it.

items.quote: what their Captain, that railing Binarius, supplieth them withall
items.note: The opponents' only weapons come from a leader the text names Binarius.

items.quote: for whose rage also and Cyclopean fury there is no other reason why it should be sent to the Isle Anticyra
items.note: Sending their rage to 'the Isle Anticyra' is figurative; the lines given do not say what the place stands for.

items.quote: their ignorance of the just and due preparation of things
items.note: Croll gives the opponents' ignorance of the right preparation of things as the cause of their rage.

items.quote: to determine of those as if we were well acquainted with them, is not only foolish, but filthy
items.note: Croll holds it wrong to judge things one does not know.

items.quote: could never find the way into Natures Sanctuary
items.note: Nature is spoken of as having a sanctuary that the school doctors cannot enter.

items.what: those eminent works wherein the whole power of Nature flourisheth
items.quote: admire, as Magical Miracles, those eminent works wherein the whole power of Nature flourisheth
items.note: Certain works are set apart as showing the whole power of Nature; the opponents take them for magical miracles.

items.quote: men skill'd in the secrets of Nature
items.note: The physicians Croll defends are those skilled in the secrets of Nature.

items.name: John
items.quote: John 5.44.
items.note: A margin reference to 'John 5.44' stands beside the passage on worldly honours.

items.name: Paracels.
items.quote: It is a wicked Tyranny to captivate the fancy of Students to certain Authors
items.note: The note points to 'Paracels. Tom. 5. in fragm. Medicis. fol. 167, 168' and goes on against binding students to set authors; the text does not show whether these words are Paracelsus's or Croll's.

items.quote: with which neither Hippocrates nor Galen, nor any Phisitians that we read of in their time were indowed or adorned
items.note: Croll notes that the ancient physicians held no doctoral titles.

items.quote: least they should be made to swear to the Heathenish errors of the School-Gods, against the naked Truth
items.note: Good physicians refuse doctoral titles so as not to be bound by oath to the schools' errors.

items.quote: they are bestowed either through flattery or bribery
items.note: Croll holds that medical titles are now given by flattery or bribery.

items.quote: they have found the brittlenesse by the losse of so noble a vessel
items.note: Interpreted: the 'noble vessel' lost appears to be the patient's body, lost through inexperienced practice.

items.quote: The Earth hideth the error of such Physitians
items.note: The grave covers up the mistakes of bad physicians.

items.name: Socrates
items.quote: as Socrates saith of rash Physitians, sport & play with mans skin
items.note: A saying about rash physicians is credited to Socrates.

items.name: Galen
items.quote: whether Galens Axioms (as he writeth) doe any more concern us, then they doe wild Bears and Bores
items.note: Words credited to Galen ('as he writeth') are turned against his own axioms.

items.quote: they are Ocularly convinced that the end doth not answer his beginning in the great Cures of Diseases
items.note: Croll holds that Galen's method fails in curing great diseases.

items.quote: the Art of Phisick is so immense and large
items.note: Croll holds that physic is so large an art that reaching it by early old age is a great blessing.

items.quote: they ought to become Schollars and servants, not Doctors and Masters of Nature
items.note: Physicians should learn from Nature as pupils, not claim mastery over it.

items.quote: God onely is Lord and Master of Nature
items.note: Margin: only God masters Nature; a degree makes no one wiser.

items.quote: like those that feed on Crabs and Crevises, they find much shell but little meat
items.note: A comparison for school learning: much outside, little content.

items.quote: Fooleries are to be forgotten.
items.note: Margin maxim; it is followed by a gap in foreign script that is not given.

items.quote: having first cast away Opinion and Scorne the lets of learning
items.note: Opinion and scorn are named as hindrances to learning.

items.quote: The world is ruled by Opinion.
items.note: Margin maxim on the rule of opinion.

items.quote: to put off their old skin, like the wise Serpent
items.note: The converts' change is likened to a serpent shedding its skin; interpreted: a figure for renewal of learning in old age.

items.what: those Secrets which are both in God and Nature
items.quote: become Schollars of Chymistry, and spend the rest of their dayes with those Secrets which are both in God and Nature
items.note: Converted physicians become scholars of Chymistry; its object is named as secrets in God and Nature.

items.quote: God is the first book that teacheth us eternall life
items.note: The margin calls God the first book, teaching eternal life.

items.name: Diogenes
items.quote: it is a lovely thing for old men to study Wisdome, and with Diogenes, not give over the Race that they are running
items.note: Diogenes is named as an example of not giving up study in old age.

items.quote: the great book of Grace, wherein the eternall health of our soules consisteth
items.note: A first book, of Grace, is set apart for the health of souls.

items.quote: more diligently to pry into that other also of Nature, treating of those Secrets which respect our bodily health
items.note: A second book, of Nature, is set apart for the secrets of bodily health.

items.quote: wherein the most High hath laid up medicines for our greatest and worst diseases
items.note: Croll holds that God has stored medicines for the worst diseases in Nature's treasures.

items.quote: The firmament or heaven with all therein is the second Naturall book conducing to a mortall life
items.note: The margin names the firmament as the second natural book; compare OPEN.19, where the second book is 'of Nature'.

items.quote: for the knowledge of Phisick is got from the Stars
items.note: Margin: medical knowledge comes from the stars.

items.quote: buried in the dead shadows of meer outsides
items.note: Outward Galenic qualities are called dead shadows of mere outsides, set against an inside not named here.

items.quote: in temporalls the chiefest thing is to find out the secrets of Nature
items.note: Margin: after eternal things, finding Nature's secrets matters most.

items.quote: they have built a stately Structure and a Temple as a most honourable monument to their old age and Nature
items.note: The converts' late learning is figured as a building and a temple.

items.quote: by their laborious examination, and Phylosophicall sequestration of the Creatures, or Naturall things
items.note: Knowledge is gained by examining natural things and by a 'Phylosophicall sequestration' of them; the lines given do not say how it is done.

items.name: Agrip:
items.quote: One shall not repent of such a Phisitian who hath the true knowledg of earthly things.
items.note: The note refers to 'Agrip: lib. 6. Epist.' beside praise of the physician who knows earthly things.

items.quote: where not many words to dispute, but much skill to cure availeth most
items.note: Croll holds that skill in curing counts at the sickbed, not disputing.

items.quote: insinuating into the richer sort for base gaine, but altogether slighting others of meaner fortune
items.note: Croll condemns physicians who serve the rich for gain and neglect the poor.

items.quote: the end of Phisick is not to scrape up money, but to discover the secrets of Nature, and the love of the Phisitian to the sick
items.note: Margin: the aim of physic is Nature's secrets and love of the sick, not money.

items.name: some of this ribble rabble
items.quote: those Phisicall Secrets, and inventions of (Chymists, which they call) Collier-like-Phisitians
items.note: The opponents' name for Chymists, 'Collier-like-Phisitians', is reported in order to reject it.

items.quote: notwithstanding they have a secret and subtle desire to learne those things which they hope to use with success and profit
items.note: Opponents who publicly forbid chemical secrets secretly want to learn them.

items.quote: robbing the Inventers of the Art, and their Benefactours, of their deserved honour by a mendacious and inverted theft
items.note: Croll accuses them of taking credit for the inventors' remedies.

items.quote: To these A pule jan Bravadoes, whether they put on the Lyons or the Foxes skin, admission to the Bath of Diana is not to be granted
items.note: Access to something called 'the Bath of Diana' is to be refused to these men; the lines given do not say what it is.

items.name: Pythagoras
items.quote: Pythagoras forbids to put our victualls into a close stool
items.note: A prohibition credited to Pythagoras is given as the reason for withholding.

items.quote: nor should we bestow our choicest herbs on such as rudely rush into the Chymists garden, seeing brambles and thistles will serve their turne
items.note: The best things of the Chymists' garden are to be kept from rude intruders.

items.quote: the flye never falls into the seething pot
items.note: Proverb-like figure; read with N035, it says slander does not touch the heroic.

items.quote: The boyling pot doth
items.note: Margin proverb on the boiling pot and flies, partly lost in gaps; it matches the 'seething pot' of OPEN.21.

items.quote: would I for the unworthinesse of some shut these doors against those that seek after the true and Ancient Phisick
items.note: Croll will not shut out honest seekers of 'the true and Ancient Phisick'.

items.quote: give place to Paracelsus according to his desert in practice and preparations
items.note: Croll holds that Paracelsus deserves recognition for his practice and preparations.

items.quote: which I intend onely against those proud, envious, ignorant vassalls, who oppose the Chymicall verity against conscience
items.note: Croll limits his attack to those who oppose 'the Chymicall verity', not to good physicians.

items.quote: before I come to describe the Remedies
items.note: Points ahead to a later description of Remedies, after the Preface.

items.quote: I handle some things in this Admonitary Preface, which with greatest intention of mind, and most diligent scruting, are to be explained by a Philosophicall Phisitian
items.note: The Preface is named and its contents announced as matters for a 'Philosophicall Phisitian'; spelled 'Admonitary' here, 'Admonitory' in the heading.

items.what: No. I: What that Phisick is which cureth mens diseases
items.quote: What that Phisick is which cureth mens diseases, and few Phisitians know it
items.note: First numbered topic; the true Phisick is said to be known to few physicians.

items.what: a perfect Philosophicall Description of the little World Man
items.quote: a perfect Philosophicall Description of the little World Man, almost forgotten and unknown
items.note: Added to No. I: a description of man as 'the little World', said to be almost forgotten.

items.quote: Where that True Phisick lyeth hid, and may be found.
items.note: No. II announces where the True Phisick lies hidden.

items.quote: That it is to be fetcht out, and prepared truly, by fire.
items.note: No. III: the Phisick is drawn out and prepared by fire.

items.what: No. IV: With what vertue ... that Phisick worketh on mans body
items.quote: With what vertue, and after what manner, that Phisick worketh on mans body, and expelleth his diseases.
items.note: Fourth numbered topic: how the Phisick acts on the body.

items.what: No. V: What manner of Phisitian that Phisick doth require
items.quote: What manner of Phisitian that Phisick doth require for its Minister.
items.note: Fifth numbered topic: the physician as minister of the Phisick.

items.what: the universall and chiefe Medicine or Phisick of the most Ancient Philosophers
items.quote: Of the universall and chiefe Medicine or Phisick of the most Ancient Philosophers
items.note: Sixth numbered topic names a universal chief Medicine.

items.quote: commended of many, possessed, yea seen, or believed of very few
items.note: The universal Medicine is said to be held or even seen by very few.

items.quote: Some thing in defence of the published Truth, as an Epilogue or Conclusion.
items.note: A closing part is announced, defending 'the published Truth'.
